chunks: And also what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Muhammad and Ahmad, the sons of al-Hasan, from their father, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

Regarding a man who dies in the month of Ramadan, he said: 'It is not incumbent upon his guardian to make up for him what remained of the month. And if he became ill and did not fast Ramadan, then remained ill until Ramadan passed while he was still ill, then died in that illness, it is not incumbent upon his guardian to make up the fasting for him. But if he became ill, did not fast the month of Ramadan, then recovered, then did not make it up, then became ill and died, then it is incumbent upon his guardian to make it up for him, because he had recovered but did not make it up, and it became obligatory upon him.'
As for what is missed by the deceased from fasting due to travel, making it up is obligatory upon him in all cases.
ai.seo_question: When is a guardian required to make up the missed fasting of a deceased person in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the juristic distinction between involuntary inability to fast (illness persisting until death) and voluntary neglect (recovery followed by death), establishing that qada is only obligatory in the latter case. It further distinguishes travel-related missed fasts, which remain perpetually due, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the guardian’s role in fulfilling the deceased’s unperformed obligatory acts (fara'id).
